The Roman notion of veritas, which emphasizes correspondence and objectifying representation, narrows this broader disclosure into a more calculable and representational understanding of truth. Modern technology inherits this narrowed sense, but it also intensifies it by revealing reality in a distinctive historical mode. The passage from a modular mod-\(p\) representation to a modular \(p\)-adic representation is the modular lifting problem. Let \(E/\mathbb{Q}\) be semistable and let \(p>3\). The residual representation \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}:G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)\) is the reduction modulo \(p\) of the \(p\)-adic representation \(\rho_{E,p^\infty}\). If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is known to arise from a weight-2 newform, one must show that the full \(p\)-adic representation also arises from a newform; by the converse theorem for elliptic curves this would imply that \(E\) itself is modular. Wiles’s strategy is to encode all possible lifts of \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) satisfying the local conditions imposed by semistability in a universal deformation ring \(R\), and to encode all modular forms with the same residual representation in a Hecke algebra \(T\). The lifting theorem is then a comparison of \(R\) and \(T\): if the natural map between them is an isomorphism, or has the required surjectivity, every admissible lift is modular, in particular \(\rho_{E,p^\infty}\).

The comparison is difficult because \(R\) and \(T\) are defined by global conditions, and one must control their ranks and singularities. Wiles, following Taylor, introduced auxiliary primes \(q\) at which \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is unramified and whose Frobenius eigenvalues satisfy a prescribed congruence. Adding these primes enlarges the level and the deformation problem, but it makes the local deformation rings at \(q\) much simpler, often isomorphic to power series rings, and allows the Hecke algebra to be computed more explicitly. By choosing infinitely many such \(q\) and using a patching argument, one shows that the enlarged deformation ring and Hecke algebra have the same structure; then one removes the auxiliary primes to recover the original statement. This is the core of the Taylor–Wiles method, and it is what turns the abstract deformation-theoretic setup into a proof of modularity.

The reducibility of the residual representation determines which deformation-theoretic hypotheses are available. If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is irreducible, the universal deformation ring is local and its tangent space is governed by a Galois cohomology group \(H^1(G_{\mathbb{Q}},S,\bar{\rho})\), so the local-global comparison is relatively well behaved; irreducibility also prevents the representation from splitting into characters and ensures that the lift is controlled by the residual data. If \(\bar{\rho}_{E,p}\) is reducible, it is an extension of two characters, and the deformation space can have several components or extra parameters. In that case the standard irreducible lifting argument may fail, and one must use additional arguments tailored to the reducible situation, often exploiting the special form of the characters and the semistable local conditions. For Frey curves arising from a putative Fermat counterexample, this distinction is essential: Wiles had to prove modularity in both the irreducible and reducible cases, with the reducible case requiring a separate treatment, before the contradiction with Ribet’s theorem could be completed.

The most plausible explanation for why hypothalamic and limbic structures such as the central bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3) can show sexually dimorphic trajectories is that brain sexual differentiation is not a single event but a set of region-specific programs. Genital differentiation is initiated early by sex-chromosome and gonadal pathways: SRY activates SOX9 in the developing testis, leading to DHH, AMH, and testosterone production, which organize the Wolffian ducts and suppress Müllerian structures. In the brain, however, the same genetic and hormonal signals are interpreted differently because neural progenitor populations express distinct combinations of androgen receptors, estrogen receptors, aromatase (CYP19A1), neurotrophic factors, and epigenetic regulators. Fetal testosterone can be aromatized locally to estradiol, and both androgenic and estrogenic signaling can influence cell proliferation, migration, apoptosis, axon guidance, and synaptogenesis in specific nuclei. In addition, sex-chromosome genes are expressed directly in the brain, and X-inactivation escape or imprinted genes may produce local effects independent of circulating gonadal hormones. Thus, BSTc and INAH3 may follow a trajectory distinct from the genitals because their critical windows, receptor densities, and local microenvironments differ from those of peripheral tissues.

Prenatal environmental mechanisms can modulate these region-specific programs without necessarily overriding genetic sex. Maternal endocrine status, stress-induced glucocorticoids, infections, nutrition, and exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals can alter the availability of steroids, the expression of aromatase or steroid-metabolizing enzymes, and the epigenetic state of neural progenitors. For example, conditions that increase fetal androgen exposure, such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or that reduce androgen action, such as androgen insensitivity, are associated with altered sexual dimorphism in some brain regions and behaviors, although the effects are probabilistic and often small relative to individual variation. Environmental influences may also act through the placenta, which expresses steroidogenic enzymes and can convert maternal and fetal steroids, creating a local neuroendocrine milieu that differs from the systemic one. Because the brain is a mosaic of cell populations with different sensitivities to hormones and different timing of development, the same prenatal perturbation can leave one structure relatively unaffected while shifting the size, connectivity, or gene-expression profile of another. This explains why brain dimorphism is not expected to mirror genital differentiation in a simple, all-or-none manner.

Nevertheless, the existence of sexually dimorphic brain structures does not demonstrate that gender identity is hardwired before birth. Studies of INAH3 and BSTc are largely postmortem, correlational, and subject to confounds such as age, cause of death, medication, and sample size; they show average group differences, not deterministic markers of identity. Gender identity is a complex, multidimensional sense of self that emerges from the interaction of prenatal biology, postnatal neurodevelopment, embodiment, socialization, language, and cultural context. Prenatal hormones and genes may create predispositions, constraints, or biases in the development of neural circuits, but they do not reduce identity to a single nucleus or a binary biological switch. The more defensible conclusion is that the brain undergoes sexually differentiated development through region-specific genetic, neuroendocrine, and environmental mechanisms, while gender identity remains a product of both biological and social processes. Thus, prenatal biology may be relevant to the origins of gender diversity, but it does not prove that gender identity is fixed, monolithic, or fully determined prior to birth.

The essential difficulty in Wiles’s argument is the passage from modularity of a residual Galois representation to modularity of the full \(p\)-adic representation. For a semistable elliptic curve \(E/\mathbb{Q}\) and a chosen prime \(p>3\), the action of \(G_{\mathbb{Q}}\) on the \(p\)-torsion \(E[p]\) gives a residual representation \(\bar{\rho}_p: G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)\), while the action on the \(p\)-adic Tate module gives a compatible system \(\rho_{p^\infty}: G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_p)\). If \(\bar{\rho}_p\) is modular, one must show that \(\rho_{p^\infty}\) is also modular, i.e. attached to a \(p\)-adic eigenform. Wiles formulates this as a deformation problem: lifts of \(\bar{\rho}_p\) to characteristic zero are parametrized by a universal deformation ring \(R\), subject to local conditions at the primes of bad reduction. On the modular side, a Hecke algebra \(T\) parametrizes modular forms whose associated Galois representations reduce to \(\bar{\rho}_p\). The modularity lifting theorem is, in essence, the assertion that \(R\) and \(T\) are sufficiently close—typically that \(T\) is a quotient of \(R\) and the two rings have the same rank—so that the elliptic-curve lift must come from a modular form.

In the irreducible case, where \(\bar{\rho}_p\) has no \(G_{\mathbb{Q}}\)-stable line, the deformation theory is comparatively rigid. The local deformation rings at the finitely many ramified primes can be controlled using the semistability of \(E\), and the global deformation ring \(R\) is finite over \(\mathbb{Z}_p\). Wiles, building on Taylor’s auxiliary-prime method, introduces extra primes at which the residual representation is unramified and the local deformation conditions are especially simple. These auxiliary primes force the ranks of \(R\) and \(T\) to agree after adding them; one then removes the auxiliary primes to obtain the desired isomorphism or equality of ranks in the original problem. Consequently, if the residual representation is irreducible and modular, the full \(p\)-adic representation is modular, and hence \(E\) is modular. This is the main lifting theorem used in the Frey-curve argument.

The reducible case requires a separate treatment because \(\bar{\rho}_p\) preserves a one-dimensional subspace of \(E[p]\), equivalently \(E\) has a rational \(p\)-isogeny. Then the residual representation is an extension of two characters, and its deformations are governed by extension classes and character lifts, which introduce additional variables and can make the universal deformation ring less well behaved. The standard irreducibility argument no longer applies directly, and this is where the original proof encountered its famous gap. Wiles’s solution, completed with Taylor, imposes the precise local conditions coming from semistability and uses a more delicate comparison of the deformation ring and the Hecke algebra, often by reducing to a situation where the relevant lifts are controlled by characters or by a compatible system. In the Fermat application, one checks which case the Frey curve falls into: if its residual representation is irreducible, the main theorem applies; if it is reducible, the reducible-case theorem still forces the associated \(p\)-adic representation to be modular. Either way, the Frey curve would be modular, contradicting Ribet’s theorem and thereby excluding a Fermat counterexample.

```python
import math
import re
from collections import Counter


def normalize(text):
    """
    Lowercase the text and replace non-alphanumeric characters with spaces.
    This keeps French accented letters while removing punctuation noise.
    """
    text = text.lower()
    text = ''.join(ch if ch.isalnum() else ' ' for ch in text)
    return re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()


def char_ngrams(text, ngram_range=(2, 4)):
    """
    Build a sparse character n-gram count vector for a normalized text.

    For each word, extract all character substrings of lengths
    ngram_range[0] through ngram_range[1].
    """
    counts = Counter()

    for word in text.split():
        for n in range(ngram_range[0], ngram_range[1] + 1):
            if len(word) < n:
                continue

            for i in range(len(word) - n + 1):
                counts[word[i:i + n]] += 1

    return counts


def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    """
    Compute cosine similarity between two sparse count vectors.

    cosine(a, b) = dot(a, b) / (||a|| * ||b||)
    """
    if not a or not b:
        return 0.0

    # Iterate over the smaller dictionary for efficiency.
    if len(a) > len(b):
        a, b = b, a

    dot_product = sum(count * b.get(ngram, 0) for ngram, count in a.items())

    norm_a = math.sqrt(sum(count * count for count in a.values()))
    norm_b = math.sqrt(sum(count * count for count in b.values()))

    if norm_a == 0.0 or norm_b == 0.0:
        return 0.0

    return dot_product / (norm_a * norm_b)


def nearest_neighbors(texts, ngram_range=(2, 4)):
    """
    Compute the closest textual match for each line in the corpus.

    Returns a list of tuples:
        (index_i, text_i, index_j, text_j, similarity_score)
    where text_j is the nearest neighbor of text_i.
    """
    # Vectorize each text into sparse character n-gram counts.
    vectors = [char_ngrams(normalize(text), ngram_range) for text in texts]

    n = len(texts)

    # Build the full pairwise cosine similarity matrix.
    similarity = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]

    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            score = cosine_similarity(vectors[i], vectors[j])
            similarity[i][j] = score
            similarity[j][i] = score

    results = []

    for i in range(n):
        # Choose the most similar line j, excluding the line itself.
        best_j = max(
            range(n),
            key=lambda j, i=i: similarity[i][j] if j != i else -1.0
        )

        results.append((
            i,
            texts[i],
            best_j,
            texts[best_j],
            similarity[i][best_j]
        ))

    return results


if __name__ == "__main__":
    corpus = [
        "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
        "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
        "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
        "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
        "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
        "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
        "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
        "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
        "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
        "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,",
    ]

    for i, line, j, match, score in nearest_neighbors(corpus):
        print(f"[{i}] {line}")
        print(f"    nearest: [{j}] {match}  cosine={score:.4f}")
        print()
```

The script first converts each literary line into a numerical representation because raw strings cannot be compared directly by vector algebra. After lowercasing and replacing punctuation with spaces, the text is decomposed into character n-grams of lengths two through four for each word. Character n-grams are especially suitable for short French verse fragments because they encode subword regularities such as prefixes, suffixes, and inflectional endings (e.g., -ment, -er, -ée) without requiring a large vocabulary or external dictionary. This representation is sparse: each document vector contains counts only for the n-grams that appear, while the implicit dimensionality is the set of all possible n-grams. Sparsity is advantageous here because the corpus is small and many lines share only a few morphological fragments; the vector space remains interpretable and computationally light.

Pairwise similarity is then evaluated with cosine similarity, which compares the orientation of two count vectors rather than their absolute lengths. For vectors x_i and x_j, the similarity is defined as cos(theta) = (x_i · x_j) / (||x_i||_2 ||x_j||_2), where the dot product sums the products of shared n-gram counts and the denominator normalizes by the Euclidean norms. Because character n-gram counts are nonnegative, the resulting score lies between 0 and 1: 0 indicates no shared subword evidence, while 1 indicates identical n-gram distributions up to scaling. Cosine similarity is appropriate for sparse textual data because it reduces the influence of document length and emphasizes lexical or morphological overlap. The script constructs a symmetric similarity matrix by computing this value for every pair i, j, then selects, for each line i, the index j != i with the maximum score as its nearest neighbor.

The nearest-neighbor result should be interpreted as a measure of surface textual affinity, not full semantic equivalence. Lines that contain similar function words, verb endings, or repeated morphemes may be ranked close even if their dramatic meanings differ. For example, a line containing “avouer” can resemble another containing “l’avoue” because both generate overlapping character n-grams such as “avo”, “vou”, and “oue”. The method is also sensitive to the chosen n-gram range: smaller n-grams capture broad phonological or orthographic patterns, whereas larger n-grams become more specific and may overfit to rare strings. Extensions could include TF-IDF weighting to downweight common n-grams, word-level embeddings for semantic similarity, or language models for contextual meaning. Nevertheless, the presented script provides a transparent, dependency-light mathematical baseline for mapping sparse French literary strings into a comparable vector space and retrieving their closest textual matches.

Circular topological fingerprints such as ECFP4 encode local molecular environments by expanding atom-centered neighborhoods to a fixed radius. In RDKit, each heavy atom is assigned an initial invariant, such as atomic number, degree, implicit hydrogen count, and chirality, and the algorithm iteratively updates each atom’s identifier by hashing the multiset of its own identifier and the identifiers of neighboring atoms within one bond. After two iterations, the identifier represents all atom environments within two bonds, the conventional ECFP4 definition. The resulting set of environment identifiers is then hashed into a fixed-length binary vector, commonly 1024 or 2048 bits. This hashing compresses an unbounded chemical feature space into a compact representation, enabling fast set operations. Because the process is graph-based and canonical, it is invariant to atom ordering and SMILES representation, but it is sensitive to local topology and atom types; it does not explicitly encode 3D geometry, conformation, or long-range connectivity beyond the chosen radius. Collisions can occur when different environments map to the same bit, so the fingerprint is a probabilistic similarity descriptor rather than an exact graph isomorphism test.

For two molecules represented as binary bit vectors A and B, the Tanimoto coefficient, also called the Jaccard index, is defined as the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union: T(A,B)=|A∩B|/|A∪B|. In terms of bit counts, if a is the number of bits set in A, b in B, and c is the number of bits set in both, then T=c/(a+b-c). The corresponding Tanimoto/Jaccard distance is D=1-T=(a+b-2c)/(a+b-c). This metric lies in [0,1], with 1 indicating identical bit patterns and 0 indicating no shared set bits. In cheminformatics, the numerator counts shared molecular substructures or hashed environments, while the denominator penalizes dissimilarities by including bits present in only one molecule. Because ECFP4 fingerprints are sparse, the Tanimoto coefficient is computationally inexpensive: it can be evaluated with bitwise AND and population-count operations, making it suitable for screening millions of compounds. The fixed bit length also allows direct comparison across molecules, although the absolute meaning of a bit depends on the hash function and fingerprint parameters.

In modern virtual screening and medicinal chemistry, Tanimoto similarity thresholds are interpreted as heuristic filters rather than universal truth values. A common rule of thumb is that similarities above 0.3–0.4 may indicate meaningful structural relatedness, values above 0.5–0.6 suggest strong scaffold or pharmacophore overlap, and values near 0.8–1.0 often correspond to close analogs or the same core structure. However, the appropriate cutoff depends on the chemical space, fingerprint type, bit length, assay, and objective. In early enrichment, a low threshold may be used to retrieve diverse actives or to perform scaffold hopping, while in lead optimization a higher threshold may be used to identify closely related compounds with predictable property changes. Similarity alone does not guarantee biological activity; it must be combined with docking scores, quantitative structure-activity relationship models, physicochemical filters, and experimental validation. Thus, Tanimoto coefficients are best viewed as a fast, interpretable measure of topological resemblance that prioritizes candidates for deeper evaluation.

```python
import random
import time


class SegmentTree:
    """
    Iterative segment tree supporting:
      - point updates
      - range sum queries over half-open intervals [left, right)
    """

    def __init__(self, data):
        self.n = len(data)
        self.size = 1
        while self.size < self.n:
            self.size <<= 1

        # Index 0 is unused. Leaves are [size, size + n).
        self.tree = [0] * (2 * self.size)
        self.tree[self.size:self.size + self.n] = data

        # Build internal nodes bottom-up.
        for i in range(self.size - 1, 0, -1):
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[i << 1] + self.tree[(i << 1) | 1]

    def update(self, pos, value):
        """Set position pos to value and update ancestors."""
        tree = self.tree
        i = self.size + pos
        tree[i] = value
        i >>= 1

        while i:
            tree[i] = tree[i << 1] + tree[(i << 1) | 1]
            i >>= 1

    def query(self, left, right):
        """Return sum over half-open interval [left, right)."""
        tree = self.tree
        l = self.size + left
        r = self.size + right
        total = 0

        while l < r:
            if l & 1:
                total += tree[l]
                l += 1
            if r & 1:
                r -= 1
                total += tree[r]
            l >>= 1
            r >>= 1

        return total


def generate_operations(n, q, rng, query_fraction=0.5, max_span=None):
    """
    Generate a synthetic mixed workload of point updates and range queries.

    Queries are half-open intervals [left, right).
    max_span limits the maximum query length to keep the benchmark practical.
    """
    if max_span is None:
        max_span = n

    ops = []

    for _ in range(q):
        if rng.random() < query_fraction:
            left = rng.randrange(n)
            right_limit = min(n, left + max_span)
            right = rng.randrange(left + 1, right_limit + 1)
            ops.append(("query", left, right))
        else:
            pos = rng.randrange(n)
            val = rng.randint(0, 1000)
            ops.append(("update", pos, val))

    return ops


def run_naive(arr, ops):
    """
    Naive continuous-array strategy.

    Point update: O(1)
    Range query: O(k), where k is the queried interval length.
    """
    checksum = 0

    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == "query":
            _, left, right = op
            checksum += sum(arr[left:right])
        else:
            _, pos, val = op
            arr[pos] = val

    return checksum


def run_segment_tree(tree, ops):
    """
    Segment tree strategy.

    Point update: O(log N)
    Range query: O(log N)
    """
    checksum = 0

    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == "query":
            _, left, right = op
            checksum += tree.query(left, right)
        else:
            _, pos, val = op
            tree.update(pos, val)

    return checksum


def main():
    N = 100_000
    Q = 50_000

    # Use a moderate maximum query span for a practical benchmark.
    # Set MAX_QUERY_SPAN = N for a worst-case-style benchmark, but it may be slow.
    QUERY_FRACTION = 0.5
    MAX_QUERY_SPAN = N // 5

    rng = random.Random(12345)

    data = [rng.randint(0, 1000) for _ in range(N)]
    ops = generate_operations(N, Q, rng, QUERY_FRACTION, MAX_QUERY_SPAN)

    query_count = sum(1 for op in ops if op[0] == "query")
    update_count = Q - query_count

    print(
        f"Benchmark: N={N}, Q={Q}, "
        f"queries={query_count}, updates={update_count}, "
        f"max_span={MAX_QUERY_SPAN}"
    )

    # Naive continuous array benchmark.
    naive_arr = data.copy()
    start = time.perf_counter()
    naive_checksum = run_naive(naive_arr, ops)
    naive_time = time.perf_counter() - start

    # Segment tree construction benchmark.
    start = time.perf_counter()
    seg_tree = SegmentTree(data)
    build_time = time.perf_counter() - start

    # Segment tree operation benchmark.
    start = time.perf_counter()
    seg_checksum = run_segment_tree(seg_tree, ops)
    seg_time = time.perf_counter() - start

    print(f"Naive continuous array operations: {naive_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree build: {build_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree operations: {seg_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree total (build + operations): {build_time + seg_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"Checksums match: {naive_checksum == seg_checksum}")

    if seg_time > 0:
        print(f"Operation speedup (naive / segment tree): {naive_time / seg_time:.2f}x")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The naive continuous-array strategy stores the sequence in a single contiguous list. A point update is Θ(1) because it replaces one array cell, while a range query over k = r − l elements must read and add every element in the interval; therefore its query time is Θ(k), with worst-case Θ(N) and lower bound Ω(k) for an arbitrary unpreprocessed array. If the workload contains Q_q nonempty queries, the total query work is Θ(Σ k_i), bounded above by Θ(Q_q N) and below by Ω(Q_q). The segment tree preprocesses the array into a balanced binary tree whose leaves hold the original values and whose internal nodes hold interval sums. Construction satisfies T_build(n) = 2T_build(n/2) + Θ(1) with T_build(1) = Θ(1), hence by the Master Theorem T_build(n) = Θ(n); equivalently, filling O(n) leaves and O(n) internal nodes is linear. A full traversal of the tree satisfies T_trav(n) = 2T_trav(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(n), but a range query traverses only the two boundary root-to-leaf paths and aggregates O(log n) canonical nodes; a single boundary path satisfies T_path(n) = T_path(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(log n), so both point update and range query are Θ(log N). The space requirement is Θ(N), because a padded tree of size S = 2^⌈log₂ N⌉ uses 2S − 1 nodes and S < 2N.

To prove the logarithmic height bound formally, let H(n) be the maximum number of edges from the root to a leaf in a segment tree built over n leaves. For n = 1, H(1) = 0. For n > 1, the root splits the interval into two subintervals of sizes ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉, so H(n) = 1 + max{H(⌊n/2⌋), H(⌈n/2⌉)} ≤ 1 + H(⌈n/2⌉). By induction, assume H(m) ≤ ⌈log₂ m⌉ for all m < n. Then H(n) ≤ 1 + ⌈log₂ ⌈n/2⌉⌉ ≤ ⌈log₂ n⌉, because halving n reduces its binary logarithm by at most one. If the implementation pads the array to the next power of two S = 2^k ≥ N, the tree height is exactly k = log₂ S. Since N ≤ S < 2N, log₂ N ≤ k < log₂ N + 1, so k = Θ(log N). Thus every root-to-leaf path, and therefore every update or boundary traversal, has length O(log N), and the Ω(log N) lower bound follows from the fact that a point update must modify all ancestors of the leaf, which are log N distinct nodes.

Although asymptotic notation favors the segment tree for long-range queries, physical hardware can invert the practical winner for small or short intervals. The naive scan is sequential, has excellent cache locality, and in Python is executed by C-level sum() over a slice, so its arithmetic constant factor is small, although the slice adds temporary allocation; for k much smaller than log N times the segment-tree constant, it may be faster. """
```python
Synthesize a 1-second C-major triad with logarithmically decaying 2nd and 3rd
harmonics, then use an FFT to extract, identify, and print spectral peaks.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import rfft
from scipy.signal import find_peaks


def harmonic_amplitude(h: int, alpha: float = 0.75) -> float:
    """
    Logarithmic decay model:
        A(h) = exp(-alpha * ln(h)) = h**(-alpha), for h > 1.
    The fundamental, h = 1, is normalized to unity.
    """
    if h == 1:
        return 1.0
    return float(np.exp(-alpha * np.log(h)))


def refine_peak_frequency(freqs: np.ndarray, mag: np.ndarray, idx: int) -> float:
    """
    Parabolic interpolation in log-magnitude around a detected peak.
    This gives a sub-bin frequency estimate for the printed peak table.
    """
    if idx <= 0 or idx >= len(mag) - 1:
        return float(freqs[idx])

    y = np.log(mag[idx - 1:idx + 2] + 1e-12)
    denom = y[0] - 2.0 * y[1] + y[2]

    if abs(denom) < 1e-12:
        return float(freqs[idx])

    delta = 0.5 * (y[0] - y[2]) / denom
    delta = float(np.clip(delta, -0.5, 0.5))

    return float(freqs[idx] + delta * (freqs[1] - freqs[0]))


def main() -> None:
    # Audio parameters
    fs = 44_100
    duration = 1.0
    n = int(fs * duration)
    t = np.arange(n, dtype=np.float64) / fs

    # C-major triad fundamentals
    fundamentals = {
        "C4": 261.63,
        "E4": 329.63,
        "G4": 392.00,
    }

    # Fundamental plus 2nd and 3rd harmonics
    harmonic_numbers = (1, 2, 3)

    # Logarithmic decay exponent for overtones
    alpha = 0.75

    x = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.float64)
    expected = []

    # Synthesize the mixed temporal signal
    for note, f0 in fundamentals.items():
        for h in harmonic_numbers:
            amp = harmonic_amplitude(h, alpha)
            f = h * f0
            x += amp * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * f * t)
            expected.append((f, f"{note} h{h}"))

    # Normalize to avoid clipping while preserving relative amplitudes
    x = 0.95 * x / np.max(np.abs(x))

    # Apply a Hann window to reduce spectral leakage
    w = np.hann(n)
    xw = x * w

    # Zero-pad the FFT for finer frequency-axis sampling.
    # This does not increase true resolution, which is ~1 Hz for a 1-s record.
    fft_size = 1 << 18
    X = rfft(xw, n=fft_size)
    mag = np.abs(X)
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(fft_size, d=1.0 / fs)

    # Peak detection parameters
    min_freq = 10.0
    min_distance_hz = 5.0
    bin_hz = fs / fft_size
    distance_bins = max(1, int(round(min_distance_hz / bin_hz)))
    prominence = 0.02 * mag.max()

    peaks, _ = find_peaks(
        mag,
        distance=distance_bins,
        prominence=prominence,
    )

    # Ignore DC and very low-frequency numerical artifacts
    peaks = peaks[freqs[peaks] >= min_freq]

    # Identification tolerance.
    # The 784.00 Hz and 784.89 Hz components are close enough that a 1-s FFT
    # may represent them as a single merged peak.
    tol_hz = 2.0

    print("Expected harmonic components:")
    for f, label in expected:
        print(f"  {label:10s}  {f:8.2f} Hz")

    print("\nDetected FFT peaks:")
    print(f"{'#':>2} {'Freq (Hz)':>12} {'Magnitude':>12}  Identified component(s)")

    detected_freqs = []

    for i, p in enumerate(peaks, start=1):
        f_peak = refine_peak_frequency(freqs, mag, p)
        detected_freqs.append(f_peak)
        m_peak = mag[p]

        matches = [
            label
            for f_exp, label in expected
            if abs(f_exp - f_peak) <= tol_hz
        ]

        ident = " + ".join(matches) if matches else "unidentified"
        print(f"{i:>2} {f_peak:12.2f} {m_peak:12.3f}  {ident}")

    detected_freqs = np.array(detected_freqs)

    missing = [
        label
        for f_exp, label in expected
        if not np.any(np.abs(detected_freqs - f_exp) <= tol_hz)
    ]

    if missing:
        print("\nExpected components not matched to a detected peak:")
        for label in missing:
            print(f"  {label}")
    else:
        print("\nAll expected components were matched to detected peaks.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) converts a finite sequence x[n] of N samples into complex coefficients X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j2πkn/N}. Each coefficient is the inner product of the signal with a complex exponential basis function of digital frequency 2πk/N, which corresponds to analog frequency k fs/N when the sampling rate is fs. The magnitude |X[k]| quantifies the strength of that frequency component, while the phase encodes temporal alignment. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) computes the same DFT in O(N log N) operations by recursively exploiting the periodicity and symmetry of the roots of unity. For real-valued audio, the spectrum is conjugate symmetric, so only nonnegative frequencies up to the Nyquist limit are retained. A window such as a Hann window is often applied before the FFT to reduce boundary discontinuities and spectral leakage; zero-padding can interpolate the displayed spectrum, but the true resolution remains governed by the record length, approximately 1/T for a T-second signal.

Psychoacoustically, timbre is the perceptual attribute that distinguishes sounds with identical pitch and loudness, and it is strongly determined by the harmonic spectrum. A musical note is rarely a pure sinusoid; it contains a fundamental plus overtones at integer multiples of that fundamental. The relative amplitudes, phases, and temporal envelopes of these partials determine whether a sound is perceived as bright, dark, nasal, reedy, or mellow. In the synthesized C-major triad, each fundamental is reinforced by second and third harmonics whose amplitudes decay logarithmically, producing a spectrum with strong low-order partials and a gradual high-frequency roll-off. The cochlea decomposes the incoming pressure waveform into critical bands, and the auditory system integrates the pattern of activated harmonics into a stable instrument-like percept. When harmonics coincide or lie close together, as with the 784 Hz second harmonic of G4 and the 784.89 Hz third harmonic of C4, their spectral energy combines, illustrating how harmonic interactions affect both the measured FFT and the perceived richness of the chord.

The time-frequency uncertainty principle, often called the Gabor limit in signal processing, imposes a fundamental constraint on simultaneous localization of a signal in time and frequency. A finite-duration window of length T produces a Fourier transform whose main lobe width is on the order of 1/T; narrowing the window improves temporal resolution but broadens the frequency response, while lengthening the window sharpens frequency resolution but smears rapid temporal changes. Mathematically, this trade-off is expressed through the product of the variances of a signal and its Fourier transform, Δt Δf ≥ 1/(4π) in the continuous case, and through the relationship between window length, spectral leakage, and bin spacing in discrete DSP. For audio analysis, a 1-second FFT can resolve frequencies separated by roughly 1 Hz, but it cannot reveal millisecond-scale attacks or decays without sacrificing frequency precision. Short-time Fourier transforms and wavelet-like methods mitigate the problem by using multiple window lengths, yet they remain bounded by the same uncertainty relationship.
